guests.heads: A group with one rule. "Send me money every month and I'll mail you a record". Pressing records for the people who made them. How a sellout led to Rounder. Working backward to John Hartford. Early on the Billy train
guests.text: If you have seen HWF on a t-shirt at a bluegrass show, you have met Kris Howland's work. A group with one rule Kris came out of the pandemic looking for company. He rejoined Facebook, joined a music group, and watched it fall apart. So he started his own, built around his own way of listening. The name began as a joke. Kris borrowed it from "Blood Sucking F(r)iends," a Greensky Bluegrass song by Dave Bruzza, where the "r" in parentheses lets you read it either way. Trevor admits he was in the group for a year before he noticed it was Fiends, not Friends. The founding rule is simple: no dunking on anyone's taste. Members post a record, name the artist and title, and talk about why they love it. Kris hits the love button even on records he would never play himself. "Nobody likes everything. Everybody loves someone. One of my buddies said that to me a few years back, and it sticks with me to this day." He hoped for 150 people to talk records with. It grew far past that. It mostly runs itself now, he says, and he still finds music there almost every day that he never knew existed. "If you can love something as much as I love my favorite things, we're solid. It doesn't matter about my feelings on it." "Send me money every month and I'll mail you a record" A member asked the group which record club he should join. Kris joked that he could send him money every month and get a record in the mail. About five weeks later, the club shipped 225 records to its first subscribers. Subscribers get one pressing a month. At first, Kris bought into runs that were already happening and added a signed card or an obi, the Japanese-style paper band that wraps the jacket. From the fourth release on, every record had to be exclusive to the club, either a color variant nobody else could sell or a pressing that existed only because the club made it. The club's catalog has since passed 50 releases. Fulfillment runs through Ridge Runner Records in Parkersburg, West Virginia, home of Kris's partner Erik Myers. Pressing records for the people who made them About half of the club's releases now are what Kris calls self-presses. He finds an artist who should be on vinyl but has no backing to get there. From mastering for vinyl to shipping, the club handles it. The first one Kris pressed himself was Kyle Tuttle's Labor of Lust , a record that was headed for CD and streaming only. The club got it mastered for vinyl, helped rework the artwork for the bigger format, and pressed it at Gotta Groove Records in Cleveland. Kyle got a stack of records for his merch table. Kris calls Kyle the mayor of progressive bluegrass in Nashville, and says doing right by him changed everything. Opportunities started coming to him through Kyle's friends. "We wanna be known as the most artist-focused label, record club, in the scene that we're all in together." How a sellout led to Rounder The bluegrass reissues started with a crash. Real Gone Music reissued John Hartford's Aereo-Plain , and a link to it landed in the group. It sold out in about half an hour. The label went looking for the source of the traffic and found a Facebook post by Kris. Gordon Anderson of Real Gone reached out. Kris, still new at this and plenty intimidated, pitched him the club. A few weeks later, Anderson came back with catalogs Kris could draw from, including Rounder, Vanguard and Flying Fish. Kris made a list on the spot. He picked records that shaped the bands he loves, and records that had become too rare and too expensive to find. Béla Fleck's Drive came first, in October 2023, its first vinyl pressing since the late 1980s. Next came J.D. Crowe & The New South , the record everyone knows as Rounder 0044, then Manzanita by the Tony Rice Unit and Doc Watson's self-titled 1964 debut on Vanguard. Rounder 0044 is personal. At Bender Jamboree in 2019, Jarrod Walker of Billy Strings's band told Kris he had to hear it before they could keep talking bluegrass. Walker wrote the set list and a note that night. It hangs in a shadow box at Kris's house. When the reissue came, Walker wrote new liner notes for it. Manzanita , pressed only once when it came out in 1979, became the club's most popular release. The goal, Kris says, is a clean, sealed copy of an essential record at a fair price, not $100 on the used market. Working backward to John Hartford Bluegrass was not something Kris heard growing up. He came to it through jam bands, Yonder Mountain String Band first, and then worked backward. He thought plenty of Hartford songs were Yonder originals before he knew better. Hartford, he says, is the trunk of his family tree on that side of his music. "A good band makes you listen to everything they've ever done. But a great band will make you listen to everything they've ever done and why they did everything that they did, all their influences." On the show, Kris broke the news of a club variant of Aereo-Plain in Cubs blue. He calls it a bit of an ego project, and a rite of passage. Early on the Billy train Kris and Trevor both caught Billy Strings early, back when you could buy a ticket at the door. The two still argue, mostly on Facebook, over whether the first pressing of Turmoil & Tinfoil came in anything other than pink. Kris stood on the arena floor in Denver not long before this conversation, watching a crowd bigger than all his early Billy venues put together. "The passion hasn't changed. The appreciation hasn't changed. It's just grown to more people."

guests.name: Lucas White
guests.dek: Bandleader of Nash Grass Unit. Founding lead guitarist of Off The Rails, the band he came on the show to talk about. A Texas guitar champion who went to Washington and helped change how songwriters get paid.
guests.bands: Nash Grass Unit. Off The Rails
guests.glance: Plays: Guitar. Started on fiddle.. From: Corsicana, Texas. Home base: Nashville, Tennessee. Titles: Texas State Guitar Champion at 15. With Off The Rails: Second place, SPBGMA band championship, 2024. First place, band contest at the Old Fiddlers' Convention in Galax and at RockyGrass, 2024. "Concrete and Steel" won the instrumental category at the Walnut Valley NewSong Showcase, 2024. On the show: Season 1, Episodes 9 and 10
guests.heads: A Texas kid on the bluegrass circuit. Tony Rice's phone number. Learning the business from the inside. The suit and the guitar. Off The Rails. Three in the morning at Galax. Nashville now
guests.text: A Texas kid on the bluegrass circuit Lucas White is from Corsicana, Texas. He started on fiddle at seven and moved to guitar as a teenager. By 15 he had won the Texas State Guitar Championship. School bent around the music. His district was persuaded that playing bluegrass counted as an education, and he got the latitude to leave in the fall for IBMA week. Summers went to Camp Bluegrass at South Plains College in Levelland and to IBMA's Kids on Bluegrass. The cost was that nobody back home knew what he was doing. "Everybody knew a Black Eyed Peas song, and they were all dancing to it in lunch or something, and I have no clue what in the world they're even referencing, because I've just been listening to Tony Rice Unit, Mountain Heart." Tony Rice's phone number He met Tony Rice in Argyle, Texas, when he was a kid. Rice gave him his phone number. "He made the mistake of giving me his phone number. I think that was like in October. And so what did I do? Thanksgiving, gave him a call. Christmas, gave him a call. New Year's, gave him a call. Easter, gave him a call." Rice took the calls, and kept taking them for years. The connection went deeper through Snuffy Smith, the luthier in King, North Carolina, who looked after Rice's 1935 Martin D-28. White spent three days at Smith's place as a young teenager, before he could drive, playing the guitar and helping put it back in order. Rice lived over in Reidsville and would turn up around midnight to see how it was going. "Here I am pounding frets into the 1935 antique Tony Rice guitar." Learning the business from the inside At 14 and 15 the producer and fiddler Jim VanCleve had him out on the road with Mountain Heart. He changed strings, flipped merch and made sure the carts were where they needed to be. Mostly he watched how the machinery worked. VanCleve has produced Off The Rails from the start. Before the band's first session he played a private show with them, so he would know how they sounded together rather than on paper. The suit and the guitar White went to Washington and worked copyright policy on Capitol Hill. He was there for the Music Modernization Act, the 2018 law that made streaming services account to songwriters and publishers, and he has worked on the HITS Act, which would let working artists write off what they spend making records. "All the societies, when they were coming in, they weren't talking to a suit or a politician. They actually did get to talk to a musician who was in a position of policymaking." He puts the motive plainly. He was making sure that when he is 70 he still gets paid for the work he is doing now. Off The Rails The band came together sideways. Cory Chubb on guitar and lead vocals, Ben Hill on mandolin and Taylor Gerber on bass were all in the Washington area when White moved up for work. Hill, a friend since childhood, pulled him into the jam. A festival offer came through White's contacts, and the group played its first gig at the Red Daisy Festival in March 2023, on Doc Watson's hundredth birthday. Billy Strings and his band played a night of Doc's music that weekend, which left a crowd primed for a jam band and nobody scheduled to be one. Off The Rails did it instead. They came off that weekend deciding it would not be a side project. Frank Evans on banjo and Cody Bauer on fiddle filled out the six-piece. Since then the band has won band contests at Galax and RockyGrass and put out singles produced by VanCleve: "Coming Home to You," "Ride Forever," written by Mason Via and Charles Humphrey III, and "She Flies," co-written by Jon Weisberger . Three in the morning at Galax "Concrete and Steel" started in a campsite at the Old Fiddlers' Convention at three in the morning, when Ben Hill put down the mandolin and picked up a clawhammer banjo. White made everybody stop and asked him to play it again. The instruments were already out, so the band built the tune on the spot. The next afternoon they played it again in the campground, and a kid and his grandmother walking the aisles stopped and started flatfooting to something that had not existed twelve hours earlier. "You have two totally different eras of people enjoying one thing together, and we created that." The tune went on to win the instrumental category at the Walnut Valley NewSong Showcase. Nashville now White makes the case that Nashville has taken the progressive bluegrass scene back from Colorado, and he has backed it with work. Approached by a bar in the Nations neighborhood about becoming its house band, he turned the slot down and built the room a weekly Saturday bluegrass night instead. He leads Nash Grass Unit, a Nashville progressive bluegrass band recording its first album. He has played the Grand Ole Opry and the Ryman and shared stages with members of the Tony Rice Unit and with Vince Herman. "It's awesome that we can feel so euphoric and almost feel like it's a drug, and get to call it bluegrass music."

On the show: Season 1, Episodes 7 and 8
guests.heads: A washed-out festival in Union Grove. The funk band. Three years with Old Crow. Songs that go to other people. Not picking a lane
guests.text: A washed-out festival in Union Grove In September 2015 Mason Via played Ancient Tones, a first-year festival held on the old fiddlers' convention grounds at VanHoy Farms in Union Grove, North Carolina. It rained hard all weekend. The campground stayed empty and the bands played to almost nobody, and Mason still talks about it as one of the good ones. It was the first time he saw Mountain Heart, The Horse Flies and Seven Handle Circus. "There was more people backstage than there were listening to the bands." That weekend came back around. Aaron Ramsey, who was on that bill with Mountain Heart, went on to produce Mason's self-titled bluegrass album, with Jim VanCleve on fiddle and Jeff Partin on bass and reso-guitar. Both are Mountain Heart alumni too. The funk band Long before the bluegrass world knew the name, Mason spent years fronting a funk band. It grew out of a friendship with Camry Harris, now the drummer for Town Mountain, who grew up alongside him and brought in players from the church scene around Martinsville, Virginia, including a sacred steel player raised in that tradition. One set of it survives on record by accident. Jon Lohman of the Virginia Folklife Program recorded the band at Rooster Walk and did not tell Mason until afterward. Mason sat on the tape for a couple of years and put it out in 2020 as Live @ Rooster Walk . "That's kinda my connection to a lot of these bluegrassers, is that we can connect on a musical level when we can realize, all right, we can play a little bit of bluegrass, but we really like to get down with the funk." Three years with Old Crow He joined Old Crow Medicine Show in 2021 as its youngest member and stayed through 2024. He had played the Opry once and cut a full album with the band before he did much of anything else in public with them. Two of the band's records topped the bluegrass chart in that stretch, Paint This Town in 2022 and Jubilee in 2023, and Jubilee was nominated for a Grammy for Best Folk Album. He headlined Salmon Fest in Alaska with them, which he counts among his favorite shows he has played anywhere. Then he left, to run his own thing. "I just want to play music and for people to hear it. And I think if the right people hear it, then it's just gonna work." Songs that go to other people His writing travels ahead of him. Molly Tuttle and Golden Highway cut "Down Home Dispensary," which he co-wrote, on City of Gold . The Del McCoury Band cut "Brown Paper Bag" on Almost Proud . He co-wrote "Ride Forever" with Charles Humphrey III for Off The Rails, the band Lucas White plays lead guitar in. He writes by hearing the finished record before it exists. "It's kind of like a silhouette of that idea in my head." When Off The Rails sent back what they had done with "Ride Forever," it matched the thing in his head. "They turned it into the thing I wanted it to be, and I didn't know if it ever even could be that." Not picking a lane Mason is not choosing a genre and staying in it. The model he names is Peter Rowan, who will turn up with a bluegrass band one night and a Tejano band the next. He has recorded an EDM track and shelved it for being too far from what he is after. His own bluegrass record moves between straight bluegrass, jam grass and Americana. "I'm trying to channel that Peter Rowan energy, the young Peter Rowan vibe." "It's always something new for the people, and I think it's fun for me, and it's fun for everyone else, too, when you push the boundaries a little bit." The Nashville rooms he named as the working ones were Dee's Country Cocktail Lounge up in Madison, where East Nash Grass, the band Cory Walker and James Kee built a Monday night into a movement, and Jane's Hideaway, the bluegrass supper club Shawn Spencer helped open. Jane's closed in 2025. Mason Via , the self-titled album he was mixing when these episodes were recorded, came out on Mountain Fever Records in April 2025. It was made in Floyd, Virginia. The IBMA nominated him for New Artist of the Year in 2026.

guests.dek: Mandolin and songs, Michael Prewitt & CrunchGrass Supreme. Three years on the road with Special Consensus. A band name born outside a Taco Bell.
guests.bands: Michael Prewitt & CrunchGrass Supreme. Special Consensus. Back Up and Push
guests.glance: Plays: Mandolin, vocals, guitar. Home base: Williamsburg, Kentucky. Albums: The Peerless Mountain Sessions (2024). Something He Can Handle (2024). Recognition: Two IBMA Momentum Award nominations, Instrumentalist of the Year. Official showcase artist, IBMA Bluegrass Ramble, Chattanooga, 2025. On the show: Season 4, Episode 33
guests.heads: A bluegrass kid in southeastern Kentucky. The North Dakota detour. The call from Greg Cahill. Two records, back to back. CrunchGrass Supreme. Next up
guests.text: Michael Prewitt grew up on traditional bluegrass, took a long detour through graduate school in North Dakota, and came back to music by way of a voicemail from Greg Cahill. Now he leads a band named after a fast food order. A bluegrass kid in southeastern Kentucky Michael grew up in the Cumberland Mountain foothills of southeastern Kentucky. His dad was a big bluegrass fan, and the house ran on cassette tapes of J.D. Crowe and Flatt & Scruggs. His middle and high school had an after-school bluegrass band sponsored by the school district, and every year the band went to IBMA. He was a self-described little bluegrass nerd. He called in to Chris Jones's show on SiriusXM and once left a voicemail in his best Lester Flatt voice, a memory that still haunts him. He met Jones at IBMA and kept in touch for years. As a teenager he found the Grateful Dead and John Hartford online, and his taste ran from traditional toward the experimental. Old time came later, in his mid-twenties. The North Dakota detour Michael earned a degree in English literature. Late in his senior year, a professor asked if he had ever thought about grad school. He had not. Then the University of North Dakota sent him an invitation, and the far north had always pulled at him. He moved there two months later, earned his graduate degree, and taught at UND for a couple of years. He spent most of his twenties in North Dakota and Minnesota. He had mostly quit bluegrass by then. The problem, as he saw it, was that no middle ground seemed to exist. "Growing up, I didn't realize that there was anything in between somebody who jammed every Friday at the cabin and Ricky Skaggs. You could either be a superstar or you could jam." In his mid-twenties he found that middle ground in the Twin Cities, which has a strong bluegrass and roots scene. He played with a regional band, Back Up and Push, and started building a working life in music. The call from Greg Cahill Around 2018 or 2019, Chris Jones put Michael on the list of fill-in mandolin players for Special Consensus. COVID canceled the tour he was booked for. Then, in 2021, band leader Greg Cahill asked Jones for a mandolin player, and Jones gave him Michael's name. Michael did not pick up the unknown number. His phone transcribed the voicemail and spelled the name with a K. He thought it was a joke until he listened. It really was Greg Cahill, asking if he wanted the gig. Michael was working full time as a mail clerk and playing a lot of gigs on the side. "It didn't take me two seconds to be like, yes, I'd love this gig." He joined in the fall of 2021. For the next three years he toured with a band that, in his words, tours as much as anyone. Two records, back to back On a Special Consensus flight, Michael was listening to the Kentucky Colonels' live records. The sound was rough and the mics buzzed, and he loved it anyway. "Here I am, 50 years later, listening to it on an airplane, and loving it. This is exactly what I needed to be hearing at this moment." That became The Peerless Mountain Sessions : a trio record of mandolin, banjo and bass, with no guitar, to leave room in the middle. Brady Wallen, a friend since high school, played banjo. Dan Eubanks, his Special Consensus bandmate, played bass. They cut it live in one day with few microphones and next to no arranging. The tunes ranged from Métis fiddle tunes to old-time Kentucky tunes and Bill Monroe. It came out in 2024 on Common Loon Records, a small label out of Dothan, Alabama. His take on "Tombstone Junction" is still his most-streamed track. That record did better than he expected, and it gave him the confidence for a bigger one. Something He Can Handle , a full-band album of mostly original songs, followed in the fall of 2024 and has earned steady SiriusXM play. CrunchGrass Supreme Michael left Special Consensus at the end of 2024, after giving a year's notice. He wanted a break from the road and more control over when, where and how he works. He moved back to Kentucky, where he teaches English online at the university in Williamsburg. The band name goes back a few years earlier. After a pickup gig at a bluegrass bar on Lower Broadway in Nashville, Michael walked past the Taco Bell on Broadway, which has its own stage and drum kit. He announced that his life goal was to play there. He would need a band for that, and a name. "CrunchGrass Supreme" came out on the spot, and he told his friends not to steal it. When dates started coming in for 2025, he never came up with anything better. "It's not maybe the best thing in the world, but at 2:00 AM sometimes it's as good as you can get." The band was an official showcase artist at IBMA in Chattanooga in 2025. At a late-night showcase that same week, he ate a Crunchwrap Supreme on stage in the middle of a song. There is video. Next up Next is his first album of all original songs, recorded by the band itself with no session players, with a fall 2026 release in view. His website lists the new collection as Poor Ol' Pitiful Human . The band has festival dates from Colorado to Missouri to Alberta to North Dakota. Michael also plays solo shows, house concerts and duo shows with bandmate Aaron Bibelhauser, and planned a three-week solo tour of England. "I'm never happier than when I'm playing music and on the road." Off stage, he collects vintage trucker hats, including a 1987 Minnesota Twins World Series cap. The Cincinnati Reds are his National League team. He also collects vinyl, CDs and cassettes, and is working through the whole Flying Fish Records catalog in order of release. Lately that means Buddy Emmons' Steel Guitar .

guests.name: Nick George
guests.dek: Not a professional musician. The friend whose taste Trevor trusts, a Portland listener who has followed Billy Strings since 2015, and what Trevor calls T Shaw's official unofficial consultant.
guests.bands: "T Shaw's official unofficial consultant," Trevor's phrase
guests.glance: Home base: Portland, Oregon. Plays: Guitar, as an amateur. Works through Bryan Sutton's bluegrass guitar course on ArtistWorks. First Billy Strings show: Wonder Ballroom, Portland, November 2015, opening for Greensky Bluegrass. Champions: Mountain Grass Unit, East Nash Grass. On the show: Season 2, Episode 16
guests.heads: Two fans, opposite corners. 2015, the opener nobody had heard of. Seven and a half hours to Boise. His case on the Billy effect. What he is pushing
guests.text: Nick George does not play for a living. He is the person Trevor texts when he wants to know whether something is worth the drive, five days out of seven, and Trevor credits him with the introduction to Luke Black and Mountain Grass Unit. He is a listener, and on this show that is the qualification. "I wouldn't say an expert in the field of all things Billy, but I'm just a crazy fan." Two fans, opposite corners They met through the Infamous Stringdusters fan base and worked out that they had come into bluegrass at about the same time by about the same route. Trevor had the southeastern advantage, a few hours from Nashville. Nick had Portland, where touring bands arrive late, arrive rarely, and arrive expensive. His answer is quality over quantity. He sees the ones that come west and streams the rest on nugs.net, after the fact if work gets in the way. 2015, the opener nobody had heard of He went to the Wonder Ballroom in November 2015 to see Greensky Bluegrass. The opener was a solo guitar player with a name Nick thought took some nerve. Ten seconds in he started working his way up from the soundboard because he wanted to see the hands. Before the set ended Greensky came out to back the kid, which Nick read as the endorsement it was. Seven and a half hours to Boise In November 2018 Billy Strings played Revolution Hall in Portland, about 900 people. The next night he was at the Olympic Venue in Boise, a room of about 300. Nick got in the car on very little sleep and made the drive. "We have to do this. We gotta go on four and a half hours sleep and drive to Boise to see this because we can't see this ever again." His case on the Billy effect Nick and Trevor disagree on one question. Has Billy Strings taken the air out of the rest of progressive bluegrass? Trevor thinks he took a large share of it. Nick does not accept a single cause. He points to inflation, to what a ticket costs now, to what touring costs a band now, and to streaming royalties that pay fractions of a penny, a framework he credits to Chris Pandolfi's podcast Inside the Musician's Brain. Package bills, to him, read as cost containment and as a way to justify coming out to a market like his. He thinks the bands still building stand to gain the most. "All this stuff is hard to measure, but I firmly believe that the net effect is going to be super positive." What keeps him going back is not technique, and he says so plainly. He can name the flatpickers he rates highest, and the draw he is describing is a different thing: a room, a following, and a door held open for everyone behind it. What he is pushing Mountain Grass Unit, the Birmingham band whose fiddler Josiah Nelson has his own episode, stayed at Nick's house on a Portland run. He talks about them as people before he talks about them as players. East Nash Grass is the current obsession, and he calls them the most underrated band on the scene. Billy Strings also sent him backward. He had not listened seriously to Larry Sparks before, and thinks Sparks belongs in the founding fathers conversation. He went deep enough into Doc Watson to walk Trevor through why Watson matters, down to the swing band with no fiddler and the decision to play fiddle tunes on guitar instead. "I am in a bluegrass cave."

guests.name: Randy Steele

guests.text: Randy is a friend of the show and its most frequent co-host. A record player and a jam band "Spoon River Breakdown" Randy Steele and The High Cold Wind June 23, 2026 0:27 Randy grew up in Bradley County, Tennessee. His grandfather loved bluegrass but could not play it. What he had was a double live album from Bean Blossom, Bill Monroe's festival, with the Osborne Brothers, Jim and Jesse and the rest of the old guard. Randy listened to it with him over and over. His own path ran through the Grateful Dead, Phish and the Allman Brothers. He played electric guitar in a regional jam band and studied studio music and jazz guitar at the University of Tennessee in Knoxville. Then he took an EMT license, went to work on an ambulance, and joined the Chattanooga Fire Department. For a few years music took a back seat. The banjo pulls him back O Brother, Where Art Thou? sent him back to bluegrass. A friend put a banjo in his hands, he found a good teacher, and he fell hard. He started on fiddle first, and he recommends it as a strategy. "Nothing is as annoying as learning how to play the fiddle, I promise you." After a year or two on the banjo, he saw Noam Pikelny play a trio show with David Grier and Shad Cobb at Barking Legs Theater in Chattanooga. It changed what he thought the instrument could do. Trevor was in the room that night too. So were the future members of Slim Pickins, none of whom knew each other yet. "Bluegrass banjo is what pulled me back into playing music. Ever since then, I've really been attached to it." Slim Pickins and the road His first bluegrass band was a weeknight picking circle with friends. When he wanted to play with stronger players, he answered a Craigslist ad for a banjo player and joined Slim Pickins. The band started playing out in 2008 and opened for the Infamous Stringdusters early on. In 2016 Slim Pickins toured Europe for about a month, playing Belgium and Holland and something like 31 shows in 28 days. The trip showed Randy how much he wanted to play live. It also formed the core of a new band. For the first half of the tour they ran as a four piece, with Randy, mandolinist John Boulware , bassist Justin Hupp and a young picker named Tyler Martelli. Songs from the Suck Slim Pickins "Cannonballs" November 15, 2025 2:17 Randy wrote most of Slim Pickins' songs, and the Europe trip pushed him to make a solo record. He cut much of Songs from the Suck at FAME Studios in Muscle Shoals and finished it near Soddy-Daisy. The title points to Suck Creek, which meets the Tennessee River just upstream of Chattanooga. Before the TVA dams, the rapids there, known as the Suck, were among the most feared stretches of the river. One song, "Mobile Soon," won the 2018 Independent Music Award for Bluegrass Song of the Year and took Randy to the ceremony at Lincoln Center in New York. The 2018 EP Moccasin Bender followed, and its song "Age of Ben" made the semifinals of American Songwriter's song contest. In 2019 he played 134 solo shows across more than 20 states while still working full time at the fire department. In 2023 he was one of 24 finalists in the Kerrville New Folk competition for emerging songwriters. The High Cold Wind After the pandemic, Randy wanted to play as much bluegrass as he could. The High Cold Wind started as the band on a record and became a working unit in 2022. Most of its members came out of Slim Pickins. The lineup now is Randy on banjo and vocals, Brad Clark on guitar, John Boulware on mandolin and Justin Hupp on bass. Lately the band has worked on opening up its jams. Randy learned to improvise in jam bands and jazz school before bluegrass, and he has pushed the band to stretch and listen harder, even running drills at practice. In March 2025 he released "The Extra Mile Is a Gravel Road," produced by Nick Lutsko. "It's about having a good time, and as long as we keep it about having a good time, I think we're in good shape." In June 2026 the band drove 1,600 miles to the Telluride Band Contest in Colorado. They made the final four, played the main stage, and finished second to the Litch Brothers of Orcas Island, Washington. Bluegrass church on Tuesdays Randy hosts a free jam every Tuesday at Barrelhouse Ballroom in downtown Chattanooga. It opens with a slow jam for beginners. He posts an eight-song set list a week ahead, mostly songs in G, C and D, so newcomers can practice. After that the floor opens to anyone. It grew fast. "We try to introduce ourselves to every person that comes in the door and treat it like a bluegrass church." Festival campground jams hooked Randy as a young player. The Tuesday jam puts that experience in public, where anyone can find it. Bringing the World of Bluegrass home When IBMA announced it would leave Raleigh, Randy sent an email to the right people in Chattanooga. He is quick to hand the credit to Visit Chattanooga, who took the idea and ran with it. WMOT later described him as the only musician on the local organizing committee that worked with IBMA. When IBMA leaders came to look at the city in late 2023, Randy made sure there was a pop-up bluegrass band waiting for them at dinner. IBMA's executive director at the time, Ken White , was one of the visitors. World of Bluegrass came to Chattanooga in September 2025. That week the High Cold Wind played Noontunes downtown and two official showcases on the Bluegrass Ramble, their first. Randy retired from the fire department as a captain earlier that year. Before the festival, Randy co-hosted two episodes with Trevor, walking through the Ramble and main stage lineups. Every photograph on this page is a frame from a video Trevor shot himself. Each one links to that moment in the video.

guests.heads: Atlanta, and a song written to a lawnmower. A house band with a rolling cast. Hideaway. The journal and the melody. "Hard Times". The blacklist on the wall
guests.text: Atlanta, and a song written to a lawnmower Before Nashville there was Seven Handle Circus, the Atlanta band Shawn fronted for several years. They climbed the Americana radio chart, got written up in Paste and Guitar World, and opened for Mumford & Sons, Better Than Ezra and the Zac Brown Band. The song that started it was "Georgia Man," and he wrote it cutting the grass. The mower held a pitch, he harmonized along with it, and by the time the yard was done he had the chorus. He was not releasing anything then. He was handing it to friends at college, and enough of them told him they loved it that he decided he was going to do this for a living. "The best songs tend to just come all at once when you're doing something random, like driving." After that band ended he made a solo record, Empty Seas , with the Atlanta producer Billy Hume. It is alternative rock, not bluegrass, and it is where the two of them learned to work together. A house band with a rolling cast He moved to Nashville in 2020 to help open Jane's Hideaway, a bluegrass supper club, and the room and the band were conceived together. Greenwood Rye started as the house band, a collective of Nashville players who rotated by whoever was free that night. He booked the rest of the venue's music too. The main cast now is David Freeman on mandolin, Taylor Shuck on banjo, Ruth Shumway on fiddle and Andy Brown on upright bass. The job he set the band was translation, not preservation. The Station Inn holds down the tradition. Greenwood Rye goes and gets the people who only know they like something about this music. "If whatever someone likes, there's a reason for it. There's something good about it. There's something that they connected with." So a night runs from old classics to Beatles songs, and the tribute shows are bluegrass tributes to Motown, to the '90s, to Paul Simon. He is not interested in policing where bluegrass stops. "It's just a word. Do we really need to argue over the definition of the word?" The band's most watched video is still a bluegrass "Everybody Wants to Rule the World," filmed around the bar at Jane's on a closed afternoon. The comments kept asking where to get the track. That is the only reason it was ever released. Hideaway Nine songs, all original, out August 23, 2024, produced, engineered and mixed by Billy Hume, who also made the Infamous Stringdusters' Silver Sky and their Grammy-winning Laws of Gravity . "Down to the River" opens it, written in the car on the Monteagle grade during the year Shawn was living in both cities. It sounds like a gospel number and is not. It is a man cheerfully expecting to be forgiven for everything, written as an answer to "Old Home Place," where nobody ever asks the girl for her side of it. "Take My Pride" came from a straighter question: what would it sound like if Mumford & Sons actually tried to write a bluegrass song. Two tracks are co-writes. "It's Not In My Blood" was written with Frank Evans, a banjo player who has subbed with Greenwood Rye plenty and spent years in the Slocan Ramblers. The closer, "Southern Pines," was written with Mason Via , formerly of Old Crow Medicine Show, at Mason's place out in Old Hickory. It was the hardest one. They moved it between time signatures, chased an idea about red dirt, and came away with two versions before Shawn took it home and assembled the one on the album. "Both people have good ideas, and then it ends up creating something that couldn't have been created without the tension." The journal and the melody He keeps two piles. Melodies go into a recorder app, usually sung as gibberish. Lines and ideas go into a journal on his phone. Writing is the work of pairing one to the other, then spilling it out as prose before it becomes verses. "Winding Road," a song about love as a journey rather than a destination, started as a journal entry called "Kudzu Love," left over from the Georgia summer camps where he runs the music. He wrote those camps a song of their own, "Where the Kudzu Grows." "Hard Times" Jane's Hideaway opened in Printer's Alley and moved across town to East Nashville in 2022. Shawn spent months of long days on the new build and had not touched an instrument in two months. He played that first Friday on the new stage, woke the next morning, and the rest of a song he had carried in the journal for years came out in one go. "Let's raise a glass and toast now that we're in a position where we can look back on the hard times and say, 'Oh, those were hard times, but let's hope they don't come again.'" Jane's Hideaway closed in June 2025 after five years. Greenwood Rye kept going, playing Nashville rooms and festivals. The blacklist on the wall There was a list on the wall at Jane's of songs the band would not play. "Rocky Top" was on it, and "Wagon Wheel," and "Tennessee Whiskey." Shawn wrote the list himself, which he admitted on the show, mostly so he had something to point at when a table wanted the band to be a jukebox. His rule is really about how the request arrives. Ask for "Man of Constant Sorrow" by its title and you have a decent chance. Ask for that song from the movie and you do not.

guests.heads: IBMA from the inside. Joining Wood Box Heroes. The Never-Ending Years. What came next
guests.text: Thomas Cassell was Trevor's first interview, back in season one. In September 2025 he came back for the show's first bonus episode, recorded ten days before IBMA came to Chattanooga. IBMA from the inside Thomas Cassell "New November" December 18, 2024 3:02 Thomas has worked IBMA's World of Bluegrass every year since 2016, including the virtual year. Some years he played 15 to 20 showcases in a week, walking from room to room with his mandolin out of the case. He also served on the education committee that sorted panel proposals and built the conference schedule. His favorite part of the business side is the Momentum Awards luncheon, where he gets to sit with friends and watch them win. The panel that changed the most for him was a 2019 session on social media. He came home and rebuilt how Circus No. 9 handled its accounts. Five months later the pandemic changed the whole internet, and he started over. "For three or four hours a day, I'm a professional. And for the other ten or so hours, I'm just totally a fan at IBMA." He likes the week for the same reason everyone does. At a festival you might see a friend for an hour. At IBMA the whole industry is in one place for days. "It's the big old family reunion, almost." When IBMA announced it was leaving Raleigh, Thomas guessed the next stop would be Knoxville or Chattanooga. He was glad to be right. Joining Wood Box Heroes Thomas joined Wood Box Heroes on mandolin in 2024, taking over from founding member Seth Taylor. The band is Josh Martin on guitar and lead vocals, Matt Menefee on banjo, Jenee Fleenor on fiddle and Barry Bales on bass. For a young band, the Grand Ole Opry came early. By the end of August 2025, Thomas had played the Opry four times with them. On the fourth, Vince Gill sat in for a song. IBMA took longer. A ramble slot opened late in the summer of 2025, and the band played its first World of Bluegrass in Chattanooga. "I have to pinch myself constantly being in there." Matt Menefee and Barry Bales were the players he watched on YouTube as a teenager. Josh Martin and Jenee Fleenor he calls two of the best musicians and front people he has ever played with. The Never-Ending Years Circus No. 9 "Chesapeake" February 9, 2019 2:05. Circus No. 9, the band Thomas founded His third solo album, The Never-Ending Years , came out on Mountain Fever Records in October 2024. He co-produced it with Casey Campbell. Thomas made a lot of phone calls for this one. There are two core bands. One is his own generation, with Jake Stargel, Cory Walker and Jason Carter. The other is what he calls his hero band: Ron Stewart on banjo, Tim Stafford on guitar and Bronwyn Keith-Hynes on fiddle. Rob Ickes, Bob Minner and Wyatt Rice sit in. The singers include Dale Ann Bradley and Missy Raines, and Ronnie McCoury sings two duets with him. Thomas was after the sound of Ronnie and Del McCoury singing together, one of his favorite things in the world. The CD comes with full liner notes: lyrics and who wrote each song. His website lists full credits for every record he has made. "When I get a record, I'm like, man, I wanna know everything about everything that's on this." What came next After IBMA 2025, Thomas played a mandolin and guitar duo set and emceed the Mayhaw Music Festival in Cottonwood, Alabama, his first time as an emcee. Then came a run of October festivals with Wood Box Heroes, including a stop in his hometown of Big Stone Gap. He told Trevor he had a solo project in the works, with duets alongside guitar players. It came out in 2026 on Common Loon Records as Guitar Collection . The photographs in the text are frames from videos Trevor shot himself. Each one links to that moment in the video.
